- [Mid-session sign-in](https://docs.mcpjam.com/inspector/lazy-authentication.md): Test servers that let you connect without signing in and ask for sign-in only when a protected call needs it

# Getting Started

> Start testing your MCP server in minutes

> [!NOTE]
>
> The upcoming SDK 10, CLI 6, and Vitest 0.3 releases require an MCPJam login or `sk_` API key for every eval, including BYOK runs with uploads disabled. These versions must ship after the backend run-start endpoint is deployed. Earlier versions keep their existing behavior.

## 1. Choose how to open Inspector

Every option below opens the MCPJam Inspector. Pick one based on where your MCP server runs.

> [card] [Web](https://app.mcpjam.com)
>
> No install. HTTPS servers only. Share servers with your team.

> [card] [Terminal](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#terminal)
>
> `npx @mcpjam/inspector@latest`. Requires Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [macOS](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#desktop-app)
>
> Desktop app (`.dmg`). No Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [Windows](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#desktop-app)
>
> Desktop app (`.exe` installer). No Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [Docker](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#docker)
>
> Pull from Docker Hub. HTTP/S, plus STDIO servers that run inside the container.

* **Your server has a public HTTPS URL**: any option works. The web app needs no install.
* **Your server runs on `localhost` or over STDIO**: use Terminal or the macOS or Windows desktop app. The web app can't reach it.
* **You want Inspector isolated in a container**: use Docker. Reach servers on your machine at `http://host.docker.internal:PORT`, and note that STDIO commands run inside the container, not on your machine.

See [Installation](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#which-one-do-i-need) for the full comparison.

## 2. Connect a server

On first launch, MCPJam shows a **Welcome** overlay that guides you through connecting your first server. You can:

* **Enter your own server** — paste an HTTPS URL (e.g. `https://your-server.example/mcp`) or a STDIO command (Terminal, Desktop, and Docker only).
* **Try the Excalidraw demo** — a hosted diagramming MCP app, no setup required.

After connecting, MCPJam shows the server name and tool count, then offers an **Open Playground** button that seeds the chat with the prompt:

```
What can this server do?
```

Press **Send** to explore your server's tools. No API key, ngrok, or ChatGPT/Claude subscription needed.

> [!TIP]
>
> You should see your server show **Connected** and its tools listed in the Playground's left rail.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.mcpjam.com/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Server Inspection

> Probe, diagnose, and export MCP server connectivity and capabilities

The `server` command group gives you a breadth-first view of any MCP server — connectivity, OAuth discovery, capabilities, tools, resources, and prompts — without writing code.

## Quick start

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
# One command does everything: probe, connect, sweep tools/resources/prompts
mcpjam server doctor --url https://your-server.com/mcp
```

If the server requires OAuth, doctor reports `oauth_required` with the discovery metadata. See [OAuth login](https://docs.mcpjam.com/cli/oauth-login.md) to obtain a token, then re-run with `--oauth-access-token`.

## Commands

### `server probe`

Stateless HTTP probe — no full client connection. Tests transport selection, OAuth discovery, and `WWW-Authenticate` parsing.

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
mcpjam server probe --url https://your-server.com/mcp
```

Use this when you want to check reachability and OAuth metadata without triggering a full MCP initialize handshake. The probe sends an unauthenticated `initialize` request and inspects the response.

**What it returns:**

* Transport type (streamable-http, SSE, or failed)
* OAuth metadata (resource metadata URL, authorization server metadata, registration strategies, scopes)
* `WWW-Authenticate` header parsing

Credential headers — `Authorization`, `X-Api-Key`, `X-Auth-Token`, and any other sensitive header names — are automatically redacted to `[REDACTED]` in the printed result. Header names are preserved so the request shape remains visible.

### `server doctor`

Combined triage — runs probe, then attempts a full client connection, then sweeps tools, resources, resource templates, and prompts. Returns a single JSON artifact.

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
# Human-readable summary
mcpjam server doctor --url https://your-server.com/mcp

# Full JSON artifact with RPC logs
mcpjam server doctor --url https://your-server.com/mcp --rpc --out doctor.json

# Stdio server
mcpjam server doctor --command node --args server.js --cwd /path/to/project
```

**What it returns:**

* `status`: `ready`, `oauth_required`, or `error`
* Probe results (transport, OAuth discovery)
* Initialization info and negotiated capabilities
* Counts: tools, resources, resource templates, prompts

From a run without credentials, `ready` means the server let MCPJam connect and list without a token. It does not mean every tool is public: a server can still ask for sign-in when a protected tool is called. To check, call that tool with `mcpjam tools call`. A 401 challenge fails the call with `AUTH_REQUIRED`, and its details name the `mcpjam oauth login` command to run. A ChatGPT-style challenge returns the tool result with `_authChallenge` next to it. See [Mid-session sign-in](https://docs.mcpjam.com/inspector/lazy-authentication.md#the-cli-tests-and-evals-never-sign-in).

The `--out <path>` flag writes the full JSON artifact to a file — useful for handoff to another engineer or agent.
For stdio targets, those artifacts only record the explicit env keys you passed
via `-e/--env`; inherited shell variables are not enumerated.

Credential headers — `Authorization`, `X-Api-Key`, `X-Auth-Token`, and any other sensitive header names — are automatically redacted to `[REDACTED]` in all printed output and written artifacts, including RPC logs attached via `--rpc`. Header names are preserved so the request shape remains visible.

### `server info`
6.2.2

# Full JSON artifact with RPC logs
mcpjam server doctor --url https://your-server.com/mcp --rpc --out doctor.json

# Stdio server
mcpjam server doctor --command node --args server.js --cwd /path/to/project
```

**What it returns:**

* `status`: `ready`, `oauth_required`, or `error`
* Probe results (transport, OAuth discovery)
* Initialization info and negotiated capabilities
* Counts: tools, resources, resource templates, prompts

From a run without credentials, `ready` means the server let MCPJam connect and list without a token. It does not mean every tool is public: a server can still ask for sign-in when a protected tool is called. To check, call that tool with `mcpjam tools call`. A 401 challenge fails the call with `AUTH_REQUIRED`, and its details name the `mcpjam oauth login` command to run. A ChatGPT-style challenge returns the tool result with `_authChallenge` next to it. See [Mid-session sign-in](https://docs.mcpjam.com/inspector/lazy-authentication.md#the-cli-tests-and-evals-never-sign-in).

The `--out <path>` flag writes the full JSON artifact to a file — useful for handoff to another engineer or agent.
For stdio targets, those artifacts only record the explicit env keys you passed
via `-e/--env`; inherited shell variables are not enumerated.

Credential headers — `Authorization`, `X-Api-Key`, `X-Auth-Token`, and any other sensitive header names — are automatically redacted to `[REDACTED]` in all printed output and written artifacts, including RPC logs attached via `--rpc`. Header names are preserved so the request shape remains visible.

The server passes validation with MCPJam CLI 6.2.2 (`mcpjam server doctor` and `mcpjam tools call`). One thing needed fixing first: `/workspace/mcp.json` has no credential, so the server returned 401 `invalid_token`.

- **Fix:** I passed `MCP_SERVER_TOKEN` with `--access-token`. I did not edit `mcp.json` or write the token to any file.
- **`doctor`:** status is `ready`. It negotiated protocol 2025-11-25 over streamable-http, found 1 tool (`add`), and no OAuth is required. The server advertises no resources or prompts, and the Skills extension was skipped, as expected.
- **`add` with valid input:** `{"a":2,"b":3}` returned `{"sum":5}` with `isError:false`.
- **`add` with invalid input:** `{"a":"x"}` returned `isError:true` with the message "a and b must be finite numbers". That is a clean tool-level error.
- **Saved work:**
  - `/workspace/doctor.json` is the full doctor report, including RPC logs.
  - `/workspace/validate.sh` reruns all three checks. It reads the token from the environment.

**Concern note:** I expected the config to connect as written, but it didn't, because it has no auth. I fixed that by passing the token on the command line. You may want to add the credential to `mcp.json`.

I didn't use the MCPJam account API or the hosted features, such as evals or project sync. The CLI checks above needed neither.
